Practical 2

Data Formats and Storage

The formats ocean data arrives in - CSV, JSON, GeoJSON and XML. One tab each: what it is good at, the whole file to read, and a copy to download.

sample_wave_buoy.csv CSV

Rows and columns, like a spreadsheet. Best for readings over time. Five days from the Honiara buoy here.

Download the CSV 

Loading...

sample_forecast_snippet.json JSON

Keys and values, nested. What an API replies with. Here daily holds parallel lists rather than rows: the first date goes with the first rainfall figure, and only their position joins them.

Download the JSON 

Loading...

sample_stations.geojson GeoJSON

JSON in a fixed shape that maps recognise. Tide gauges here, each with properties and a geometry. Coordinates are longitude first - the usual reason a station appears in the wrong ocean.

Download the GeoJSON 

Loading...

sample_station_metadata.xml XML

Nested tags. The usual choice for metadata - what the instrument is, not what it recorded. Installed, last serviced, still active: that is how you tell a fault from a service visit.

Download the XML 

Loading...

Your turn - plot the data with Python

plot_wave_buoy.py is in this folder, next to the CSV it reads. It cleans the readings and draws wave height and peak period.

Run it in the terminal:

pip install pandas matplotlib
python plot_wave_buoy.py

The whole script

Read it top to bottom - it is the same five steps every plotting job has: load, check, clean, order, draw. Coloured the way your editor would colour it: comments grey, text in quotes one colour, keywords another.

You can type in the box below. Click into it and edit, then click away and the colours redraw. Nothing here is saved to the file - it is for trying an idea before you change the real script. Reset puts it back.

Step 2 is the one to linger on. The two bad readings you found on the CSV tab are removed there - comment those lines out, run it again, and see how badly one 99.9 distorts the whole chart.

What it printed

The print lines in the script, in the order they ran. This is the quality check: one dropped reading, one sensor error, both found before anything was plotted. 

$ python plot_wave_buoy.py
First few rows:
          timestamp            station  latitude  longitude  hs_m  tp_s
0  2026-08-01 00:00  Honiara Wave Buoy     -9.45     159.96  0.92   6.8
1  2026-08-01 03:00  Honiara Wave Buoy     -9.45     159.96  0.88   6.6
2  2026-08-01 06:00  Honiara Wave Buoy     -9.45     159.96  0.95   7.0
3  2026-08-01 09:00  Honiara Wave Buoy     -9.45     159.96  1.05   7.2
4  2026-08-01 12:00  Honiara Wave Buoy     -9.45     159.96  1.18   7.4

Rows with a missing wave height:
          timestamp            station  latitude  longitude  hs_m  tp_s
9  2026-08-02 03:00  Honiara Wave Buoy     -9.45     159.96   NaN   6.7

Rows with a suspicious wave height (over 10 m is not possible here):
           timestamp            station  latitude  longitude  hs_m  tp_s
22  2026-08-03 18:00  Honiara Wave Buoy     -9.45     159.96  99.9  13.1

Saved plot to wave_buoy_plot.png

NaN is how pandas writes "no value here" - the blank cell in the CSV. Notice the 99.9 row also has a tp_s of 13.1 seconds, which is high but possible: only one of the two readings failed, which is why the check is on hs_m alone.
